properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-21: "does each of the 10 subsystems have a defined interface contract? this is probably related to the tests for each subsystem. I had mentioned at some point that it would be nice to able to swap out a module for another (related to MOSA), but that is only possible if you defined contracts for each module/subsystem. I also feel like if you have defined contracts, you could mock its behavior for testing purposes."

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THE ANSWER TO THE DIRECT QUESTION: NO — ZERO OF TEN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

FOUR of the ten subsystems declare a provided interface at all. Of those four:
  sys:foundation    -> ifc:core-api       spec = a 2026-07-28 note saying the old `medium: REST` was a schema default and wrong
  sys:store         -> ifc:graph-export   spec = the same kind of correction note
  sys:human-channel -> ifc:reasoning-channel   NO SPEC
  sys:time-history  -> ifc:temporal-api        NO SPEC

Both "specs" are PROVENANCE CORRECTIONS. They are true and useful and they name no operation, no input and no output. **Not one subsystem publishes something you could substitute against or mock from.** The other six provide nothing.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN LAZY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    designation   count   with a substantive spec
    required        9            9  of 9
    published       4            2  of 4   (the other two are correction notes)
    internal        4            0  of 4

REFLOW2 HAS WRITTEN CAREFUL CONTRACTS FOR EVERYTHING IT DEPENDS ON AND ALMOST NONE FOR WHAT IT OFFERS. That is not an oversight anyone made; it is what happens by default. You specify what you CONSUME because you must know what to expect from someone else. You leave what you PROVIDE unspecified because you are on both sides of it and nothing ever forces the question. `internal` — module to module, exactly where a swap would happen — is 0 of 4.

⭐ AND THIS IS PRECISELY WHAT BLOCKS BOTH THINGS HE NAMED. Substitution matches what a module OFFERS. A mock stands in for what a module offers its callers. Both need the PROVIDED side specified, and the provided side is the side nobody wrote.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ ONE MISSING THING, NOW TRACEABLY THREE RETURNS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  1. SUBSTITUTABILITY / MOSA        — swap a module that meets the contract (2026-08-20)
  2. DERIVABLE FAILURE-MODE TESTING — edge cases from input boundaries, failure modes from output promises (2026-08-20)
  3. MOCKABLE TEST DOUBLES          — NEW TODAY, and the cheapest of the three to demonstrate

All three are blocked by the same gap, and the gap already has a number: 192 capabilities, 3 declaring inputs, 3 declaring outputs, 0 declaring a signature. `set_capability_signature` EXISTS and is verified — it was built precisely because the fields were unwritable at 0 of 170. It is now used on 3 of 192. **The TOOL leg is built. The INSTRUCTION and the DETECTOR are not.**

📌 MOCKING IS THE SHARPEST ARGUMENT OF THE THREE and it is worth saying why. Substitutability is a someday benefit — nobody is swapping the store this quarter. Derivable tests are a maybe: it is still unmeasured whether declared inputs produce cases nobody had thought of. **A mock pays immediately and locally**: a test that stands `sys:store` up against a fake instead of a real RocksDB is faster, and it is the only way to test the failure modes of a dependency you cannot make fail on demand. It is also the return with the shortest path to proving the contract is REAL — a contract you can mock is one you have actually specified, and a mock that diverges from the real module is a contract violation you can detect.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑 A REAL TENSION, RECORDED RATHER THAN RESOLVED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Earlier reasoning held that six subsystems present nothing BECAUSE NOTHING CONSUMES THEM, and that declaring interfaces for symmetry would FABRICATE CONTRACTS — asserting an agreement no two parties ever made. That argument is good and it is still good.

His MOSA argument cuts the other way: a contract is what makes substitution possible, so it is needed whether or not anything consumes it TODAY. An interface nobody consumes is not a fiction if the point of writing it is that someone else could implement it.

**BOTH ARE RIGHT ABOUT DIFFERENT THINGS.** The fabrication risk is real for a CONSUMES edge — that asserts a relationship. It is much weaker for a PROVIDES spec, which asserts only "this is what I offer", a statement the module can make alone and be held to. That distinction is not currently drawn anywhere, and drawing it may dissolve the tension entirely.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THE OPTIONS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

(a) SPECIFY ONE SUBSYSTEM'S PROVIDED CONTRACT AND MOCK IT. `sys:store` is the candidate: 2 components, it already provides `ifc:graph-export`, and it is the dependency most worth faking in a test (real RocksDB is the slowest thing in the suite). Write the spec, build a mock against it, and see whether the mock catches anything. SMALLEST THING THAT PROVES ALL THREE RETURNS AT ONCE, because a contract you can mock is one you have really written.

(b) THE THREE LEGS FOR CAPABILITY SIGNATURES. Instruction plus detector for `inputs`/`outputs`, since the tool exists. Cheap, and it moves 3-of-192 rather than answering a question. It is the ENABLER for (a) at scale but proves nothing on its own — and building the legs before knowing the vocabulary earns its keep is how 189 empty fields happen twice.

(c) DECLARE THE MISSING PROVIDED INTERFACES for the six silent subsystems. Directly answers his question. RISKS exactly the fabrication the earlier reasoning warns of, unless the provides-versus-consumes distinction above is settled first.

(d) MEASURE WHETHER A CONTRACT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT ANYTHING. Take the last N real defects and ask how many a specified provided interface would have prevented or caught. Answers "is this worth it" before any of the above, and it is the option that could kill the whole line of work honestly.

NOT KNOWN: whether reflow2's own architecture even permits module substitution. Nearly every function is an `impl DesignGraph` method on one shared struct — which is also why attributing a test to a module mechanically was so hard today. A design where everything hangs off one god-struct may be UNSWAPPABLE regardless of what contracts get written, and that is measurable before committing to any option here.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ EXTENDED 2026-08-21 — OPTIMISATION IS THE FOURTH RETURN, AND HE RATES IT ABOVE SUBSTITUTABILITY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

HIS WORDS: "the other thing I'd like to do is optimize. I feel that this is much easier if you do this internal to a module and one by one. if you have a contract with other modules, then you can really focus only on the internals of your black box (I think technically this is a white box since you can see what's inside). you can optimize one module at a time. this is probably more important than being able to swap out a module for another, but still the same principle."

📐 HIS TERMINOLOGY POINT IS CORRECT AND WORTH KEEPING. Black box and white box are the same element seen from the two sides of one contract. SUBSTITUTION is the black-box activity — you replace the inside and only the contract matters. OPTIMISATION is the white-box activity — you keep the contract and rework the inside. **They are duals across the same boundary, which is why one contract buys both.** The design carries `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (accepted) and has no complementary word for the other view; nothing breaks without one, but the pairing is worth naming because it explains why these two returns arrive together.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑🛑 BUT A CONTRACT IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SO PLAINLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Optimising one module needs THREE things. The contract is only the first:

  (i)   A WALL — so a change to the inside cannot leak out.
        STATUS: 0 of 10 subsystems publish a contract (measured above).
  (ii)  A TARGET — what "better" means, and when to stop.
        STATUS: 1 Constraint in the entire design, and it is a SEMANTIC limit
        ("what complementary-pairing can ever catch"), not a budget.
        0 DimensionAssessments. **There is no stated performance target anywhere.**
  (iii) A MEASUREMENT — so you can tell whether you improved anything.
        STATUS: no benches directory, no criterion dependency, and not one
        `Instant::now()` or `elapsed()` in any test or tool. **Nothing in this
        repository measures how long anything takes.**

⭐⭐ AND THE ORDERING IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE INTUITION IN HIS MESSAGE. You CAN optimise a module with no contract, given a target and a measurement — people do it every day; they just risk breaking a caller and finding out later. You CANNOT optimise with a contract and no measurement: you can only change things and believe you improved them. **So for OPTIMISATION the contract is the LEAST urgent of the three, even though for SUBSTITUTION it is the most urgent.** The two returns want the same contract but not in the same order, and doing contracts first because they serve both would put the cheapest missing piece last.

📌 THIS IS ALSO WHERE HIS OWN OVER-ENGINEERING CONCERN BITES HARDEST. Optimising without a stated target is the definition of gold-plating: there is no condition under which you are finished, so the work ends when attention runs out. A budget is what makes optimisation STOP. `Constraint` + `budget_report` is exactly that machinery, built, and used once — on something that is not a budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
📐 AND ISOLATION IS PARTIAL HERE FOR A REASON THAT IS NOT ABOUT CONTRACTS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    54 core modules
    43 of them add methods to the SHARED `DesignGraph` struct (58 impl blocks)
    42 of them DO define types of their own

So modules own their OUTPUT types and not their STATE. Every one reads the same store through the same accessors. That means the internals a module can freely rework are its ALGORITHMS, and the internals it cannot are its DATA REPRESENTATION — changing how detection stores or indexes anything touches everybody. **Which caps what "optimise one module at a time" can reach**: constant factors and query shape, yes; a different index or layout, no. A contract at the seam does not change that, because the coupling is through shared state rather than through the interface.

⇒ A FIFTH OPTION FOR THE LIST ABOVE:

(e) GIVE ONE MODULE A TARGET AND A MEASUREMENT, AND OPTIMISE IT. Pick the slowest thing in the suite, state a budget as a `Constraint`, measure it, improve it, and see whether the budget was what made the work stop. CHEAPEST OF ALL THE OPTIONS — it needs no contract, no schema change and no new vocabulary, and it exercises `Constraint` + `budget_report`, which stand at 1 use. It also produces the first performance number this project has ever had, which every other option here would eventually need.
properties.name: OPEN — zero of ten subsystems publish a contract. Would writing one buy substitution, derivable tests, a mock, or optimisation?
